newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - US bank reform faces shrinking middle ground.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - US bank reform faces shrinking middle ground.

text.p: Efforts to overhaul antiquated U.S. banking laws could come grinding to a halt this week as lawmakers struggle to find a compromise approach on several unresolved issues.
Most agree that Depression era laws separating banking from other financial service industries should be scrapped.
But there is continued, heated debate over regulating bank insurance activity, allowing banks to engage in nonfinancial businesses, and the future of the savings and loan industry.
The House Banking Committee begins formal consideration of bank reform on Tuesday with dozens of amendments expected.

Committee members will work from a final draft bill completed on Friday by chairman Jim Leach, Republican of Iowa, which combined elements of three earlier bills with parts of the Clinton administration's reform plan.

Leach said on Monday that prospects for passing reform this year are better than before. But, "prospects are always dicey," he told Reuters Financial Television. "To get all the parties together and also make sure the public interest is advanced is a very difficult art form."
Analysts and lobbyists were even less optimistic.

"I don't think they're going to be able to get a bill out of committee," industry analyst Bert Ely, president of Ely & Co, said on Monday. "There are going to be at least 100 amendments, maybe more. Tempers are going to flare. It's a guaranteed recipe for something collapsing."
"Between what we need and what we can't live with, there's not much wiggle room, if any," one bank lobbyist said.
For more than a decade, Congress has sought to reform the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act but the efforts have always broken down when the major industries could not reach a consensus.
This year, lawmakers felt added pressure as industry and regulatory developments shook the existing legal framework.
In 1996, the Supreme Court, the Federal Reserve and the Comptroller's Office gave banks more leeway to expand into securities and insurance, while those industries remain locked out of banking.

Banks have been snapping up securities firms at a rapid clip. Last week, BankAmerica Corp said it would buy California investment bank Robertson Stephens & Co, following similiar acquisitions by Bankers Trust New York Corp and Swiss Bank Corp.

Ahead of Tuesday's session, banks objected to several provisions in the final Leach bill, which allow state regulation of bank insurance sales, while insurers complained the bill lacked adequate consumer protection laws governing banks.

And at least one top federal bank regulator, Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig, agreed with the banks. In a memo circulated to Congress, Ludwig's office said the bill vested too much authority over banks with non-bank regulators.
The comptroller's office "would lose the deference traditionally given to it with respect to insurance, securities and firewalls," the memo noted.
Jeff Myers, spokesman for the Independent Insurance Agents of America, said the group hoped its concerns could be addressed, but "nobody's holding their breath."
A majority of the banking committee is said to be favoring a compromise approach on commerce banking. Leach's bill omits the issue, but several amendments are expected.
The leading approach would allow financial companies that own banks to conduct up to five percent of their business in non-financial activities.
That is considerably lower than a 25 percent "basket" limitation included in a bill introduced by Republican Marge Roukema of New Jersey and Democrat Bruce Vento of Minnesota.
But it is still too much for some opponents of mixing banking and commerce. "It opens the door to a slippery slope," Ken Guenther of the Independent Bankers Association of America said.

Republican Bill McCollum of Florida is expected to introduce an amendment to allow any basket limitation to apply in reverse to commercial companies. Under the five percent rule, for example, a commercial company could get five percent of its revenue from banking activities.

Commercial banks are also worried about savings and loans. Under Leach's final draft, the federal thrift charter and the Office of Thrift Supervision would be eliminated, but banks would not gain all of the perquisites thrifts currently enjoy.
That outraged the thrift industry, which backs an amendment to strike Leach's thrift provisions expected from Democrat John LaFalce, Democrat of New York, and Jack Metcalf, Republican of Washington.
Bank lobbyists said they would not support a bill that preserved the federal thrift charter.
